title: Building Leadership Through Associations: A Conversation with Loida Garcia-Febo
raw_text: How can library associations strengthen leadership and help library and information professionals respond to increasingly complex and uncertain environments? On 25 June 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair of the IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) , joined a conversation with Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair of the IFLA Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Division , and Nick Boxem, Chair of the IFLA Europe Regional Division , both members of the IFLA Regional Council leadership group. The conversation explored leadership within IFLA and library associations, and how strategic planning, capacity building and professional networks can help organisations and individuals respond more effectively to change. Leadership is a capacity that can be developed Leadership is not simply linked to holding a formal position but it is a capacity that can be intentionally developed through experience, training, mentoring, coaching and opportunities to work with others. For library associations, this means creating environments where current and emerging leaders can learn, test ideas, build confidence and develop the skills required to guide organisations through change. Garcia-Febo highlighted the importance of leadership training, mentoring and coaching, alongside team building and effective communication. Onder haar leiding behaalde Bibliotheek Utrecht in 2025 de titel Beste Bibliotheek van Nederland . Daarnaast kreeg ze veel lof voor het grensverleggende project ‘Het Boekenspektakel’. title: Samenwerking bibliotheek Gelderland Zuid (Nijmegen) met eigenaren minibiebs
raw_text: Nijmegen telt honderden minibiebs, de kleine boekenkastjes die je in de straat vindt. Bibliotheek Gelderland Zuid/Bibliotheek Mariënburg (OBGZ) besloot samen te werken met de eigenaren van deze minibiebs, als opstap naar de bibliotheek. Wouter van Balveren, innovatiemanager bij OBGZ (Nijmegen en omstreken) vertelt aan Probiblio.nl dat de bieb de kleine boekenkastjes niet als bedreiging ziet, maar juist als stimulans. ‘De eigenaren zijn enthousiaste mensen die van lezen houden en het leuk vinden om boeken en verhalen met anderen te delen. In die zin zijn het eigenlijk ambassadeurs van leesplezier, net als wij. Daarnaast past het goed bij onze missie: wij staan voor leesplezier, verhalen en toegang tot boeken voor iedereen.’ OBGZ ziet de minibiebs dus als een soort opstap naar de bibliotheek. ‘Wij proberen natuurlijk met onze vestigingen in allerlei wijken zichtbaar te zijn, maar minibiebs zitten echt in de haarvaten van de samenleving. Die staan gewoon in woonwijken, soms bijna in iedere straat.’ De Nijmeegse bibliotheek ondersteunt de minibiebs op verschillende manieren. ‘We kijken naar waar wij als openbare bibliotheek iets kunnen toevoegen. Dat kan collectie zijn, maar ook praktische ondersteuning of ontmoeting.’ De eigenaren hadden volgens Van Balveren behoefte aan drie dingen: collectie, fysieke ondersteuning en inspiratie en ontmoeting. title: Digital Preservation: Internet Archive Releases Online Archive (199,000 Articles) of BET Journalism No Longer Available on the Live Web
raw_text: From the Internet Archive (via Bluesky, X, and Mastodon): Much of BET’s digital journalism is no longer available on the live web. Internet Archive has preserved more than 199,000 BET articles over the years. They can now be accessed through The Wayback Machine & a new pilot explorer: https:// wayback-labs.sf.archive.org/bet-explorer/ Background From Huff Post: Black Entertainment Television, more commonly known as BET, has removed all digital articles from its website in a push to prioritize video content, HuffPost’s Phil Lewis reported Friday. Multimedia reporting remains on the site and BET’s social channels. However, the move to erase the written content came without warning, leaving many writers with no trace of their work, Lewis reported. “Years of news articles are now gone forever,” he wrote. While BET was once known as the pinnacle of Black media, its decision to remove these digital articles adds to an already fragile state of journalism, especially the Black press, as the Trump administration continues to target press freedom and diversity, equity and inclusion. title: New Freckle Project Report Examines 15 Years of Public Library Use
raw_text: From EveryLibrary Institute: A new Freckle Project Report, “15 Years of IMLS Figures” , looks at national public library statistics from 2010 through 2024 and identifies a striking contrast: American public libraries have more facilities, more staff, and higher levels of funding than at any point in the period examined, while several major measures of physical library use remain substantially below their 2010 levels. The Freckle Project is led by researcher Tim Coates, and its publication is supported by the EveryLibrary Institute. The August 2026 Report examines 15 years of data from the Institute of Museum and Library Services on America’s public libraries. In 2024, the United States had 17,580 public library facilities and 147,289 library employees, while public libraries received nearly $18 billion for operations and another $1.6 billion for capital expenditures. Yet annual visits declined from approximately 1.57 billion in 2010 to 869 million in 2024, while total circulation fell from approximately 2.47 billion to 1.71 billion. Coates’s analysis highlights an especially significant decline in adult physical circulation. After subtracting electronic and children’s circulation from total circulation, he estimates that this category fell approximately 68 percent between 2010 and 2024. title: Bibliothecaris VS die zich verzette tegen LHBTQ+-censuur ontvangt schikking na ontslag
raw_text: Saline County in het Amerikaanse Arkansas moet 275.000 dollar betalen in een zaak tegen een bibliotheekdirecteur die zich verzette tegen censuur van LHBTQ+-boeken op de kinderafdeling. Ze werd daarop ontslagen. Een burgerrechtenorganisatie spande een rechtszaak aan en het kwam tot een schikking. Burgerrechtenorganisatie ACLU van Arkansas greep in toen directeur Patty Hector in 2023 was ontslagen vanwege haar kritiek op een verordening die voorschreef dat boeken met ‘seksuele inhoud of afbeeldingen’ uit de kinderafdeling moesten worden verwijderd. ‘Zwijgen nooit de oplossing’ ‘Het opkomen voor de vrijheid om te lezen heeft me mijn baan gekost, en de carrière waar ik zo van hield, maar ik heb nooit geloofd dat zwijgen de oplossing was’, zegt Hector tegen Advocate .com . ‘Bibliotheken zijn van iedereen. Bibliothecarissen moeten hun gemeenschap volgens professionele normen van dienst kunnen zijn, zonder bang te hoeven zijn voor politieke represailles. Ik hoop dat deze schikking een signaal afgeeft aan bibliothecarissen en andere ambtenaren in heel Arkansas dat hun stem en hun grondwettelijke rechten ertoe doen.’ Hectors ontslag viel samen met een Amerikaanse conservatieve campagne om de toegang tot boeken te beperken, waaronder veel titels met LHBTQ+-thema’s. Hector stelde destijds dat deze boeken niet als ongeschikt voor kinderen mogen worden beschouwd. ‘Het is niet illegaal om homo of trans te zijn’, zei ze tijdens een openbare hoorzitting. title: IFLA Europe Regional Division Webinar 2026: How EURDC supports Libraries across Europe
raw_text: The IFLA Europe Regional Division invites library professionals, information specialists, and IFLA members from across Europe to an engaging online webinar on 1 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST . Over the past five years, the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) has worked to strengthen collaboration, advocacy, and engagement among libraries and library professionals throughout Europe. Despite these efforts, many colleagues remain unfamiliar with the division’s mandate, activities, and opportunities for involvement. This webinar aims to change that. During the session, four members of the current EURDC Committee, representing Finland, Germany, Norway, and Portugal, will introduce the division’s work and share practical examples of how EURDC supports the European library community. Participants will gain insights into the division’s objectives, ongoing initiatives, and future priorities. The webinar will also provide an opportunity for dialogue. Attendees will be encouraged to share their expectations, discuss challenges facing libraries in Europe, and suggest ways in which EURDC can better support their work and professional communities. The event will be conducted in English via Zoom, with automated subtitles available to improve accessibility. title: The Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) WLIC 2026 Outcomes Report
raw_text: Part of MLAS Members and Attendees at MLAS Business Meeting in Busan The IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) had an active and substantive presence at the IFLA World Library and Information Congress (WLIC) 2026 in Busan. Activities included the MLAS Business Meeting, MLAS Open Session, IFLA Associations Meeting, an informal meeting of International Relations Chairs, and opportunities for congress attendees to connect with the MLAS Chair at the IFLA exhibition booth. Across these activities, common priorities emerged: strategic renewal, member engagement, leadership, partnerships, advocacy, financial sustainability, visibility, digital transformation and AI, resilience, crisis preparedness, and responsiveness to changing societal needs. These priorities are closely aligned with MLAS’s mission to support strong, well-managed library associations through leadership, peer learning, resource development, and effective association practices worldwide. Strong library associations do not simply have strategies. They make their strategies visible, translate them into action, engage their members, build partnerships, advocate effectively, develop new leaders, sustain their organisations, and continually renew themselves in response to change. title: Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries (New Journal Article)
raw_text: The article linked below was published by Public Library Quarterly. Title Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries Authors Kathryn FitzGerald University of Washington Benjamin Lee University of Washington Source Public Library Quarterly DOI: 1 0.1080/01616846.2026.2725502 Abstract As artificial intelligence reshapes both library work and the information environment, public libraries must determine whether or how to engage with AI while maintaining library values. To our knowledge, there exists no published analysis of how American and Canadian public library AI policies might link library values and technology adoption. To address this gap, we conducted an environmental scan of public library websites to identify and analyze AI policy statements. Our scan of over 200 library websites identified 32 AI polcies. All reference at least two values, with privacy, security, and responsibility the most frequently cited. Some satellite companies still have an appetite for boutique launch services
raw_text: If you ask most satellite companies aside from SpaceX, they will tell you the world doesn't have enough capacity for launching payloads into orbit. This is despite the blistering launch cadence we've seen around the world in recent years, led by SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket. Customers in any sector will, of course, usually welcome competition. Theoretically, competition will lead to lower prices and allow the best to rise to the top. It seems like the customers buying launch services were right. SpaceX is dialing back its Falcon 9 launch program , and there is no certainty about when SpaceX's reusable next-generation super-heavy-lift rocket, Starship, will carry anything to orbit besides the company's own Starlink satellites. So it's no surprise satellite operators are cheering the success of a new launch provider. This was especially the case a few days ago, when Germany's Isar Aerospace reached orbit for the first time with its Spectrum rocket. The launcher delivered a batch of CubeSats to low-Earth orbit from a spaceport in northern Norway, and Isar tasted success after its first test flight ended in failure last year. title: Random rewards enrich classic game-theory insights
raw_text: Games may be life with all the hard bits removed, but they provide a way to study why people make the choices they make. Traditional games are usually played against a static background: the rewards per outcome are constant. That limits their relevance to behavior because, in real life, the rewards and consequences of strategic choices are ever changing. Now, researchers have used a mathematical model to study a series of games that include evolving strategies and randomly varying returns. A bit of history Perhaps the most famous game-theory contest is the prisoner’s dilemma. In the prisoner’s dilemma, a pair of thieves have been captured and are being separately interrogated by the police. If both clam up, they will be punished for a lesser crime. If one prisoner makes a deal (defects) then that prisoner gets to go free and the other gets a heavier sentence. If both make a deal, they both get an in-between punishment. The person running the game can start it with different rewards for cooperating and defecting to explore how the optimum strategy varies with reward and risk, which the players can figure out by varying the strategies across multiple rounds. Depending on the balance between the reward for staying silent (cooperating) and betrayal, the game stabilizes with everyone betraying everyone. In this simple situation, everyone loses. Bouncy castle launches horrifying MRSA outbreak, striking 48 kids in Ireland
raw_text: For a child bursting with energy, few things are more fun than hurtling through a bouncy castle, launching into the air, and ping-ponging between every surface. But that childhood buoyancy will quickly deflate when it turns out those surfaces are smeared with a hypervirulent, multidrug-resistant pathogen. That was the horrifying reality for a community in Ireland in fall 2025. Neighbors had gathered for an afternoon of merriment, complete with a barbecue, a sweets station, and three bouncy castles. Officials estimate that about 120 people joined the festivities, and around half of them were children and teens. Within a day, some children began developing signs of an infection. In all, 48 children in the community developed aggressive skin and soft-tissue infections. Of the 48 cases, 33 were treated by their regular doctor, and 15 sought emergency care. Four children ended up being hospitalized. Luckily, all of the children recovered. The results of the outbreak investigation were reported this week in the journal Eurosurveillance . title: Trump's forced coal plant extensions thrown out by judge
raw_text: The use of coal to generate electricity on the US grid has been plunging for nearly two decades, and the first Trump administration was unable to affect the trend. So his second administration has attempted more aggressive interventions to prop up coal use. One of its most direct means of doing so is to order coal plants that were scheduled to close to remain open , even if there is no need for them . The administration's justification for these orders is a statute that allows the Department of Energy (DOE) to declare an emergency in the case of wartime or a sudden shortfall in generation. A number of parties, including states where coal plants have been slated to close, have challenged this declaration. And on Friday, in the first of these cases to make its way through the courts, the declaration was judged to be contrary to the statute. While this only affects a single coal plant in Michigan, the reasoning of the decision will apply to every coal plant closure that has been blocked by the DOE. Campbell Generating Plant, which was scheduled to close last year but has been kept open by a total of five emergency declarations by the DOE, each limited to 90 days by the Federal Power Act. title: ChatGPT-using lawyer punished for citing fake testimony from made-up witnesses
raw_text: The New Mexico Supreme Court held a ChatGPT-using lawyer in direct contempt of court for submitting a brief with "false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses," including fake police testimony and other mistakes. The state's top court referred the lawyer to a disciplinary board for further proceedings and concluded that he "demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client." Attorney Stephen Aarons "admitted to the Court that he did not verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief before signing it and filing it with the Court, and that he did not inform his client of this failure or that the brief in chief contained multiple factual and legal misrepresentations," the state Supreme Court said in an order on Wednesday. Aarons has been a criminal defense lawyer in New Mexico for over 40 years and was hired by a defendant's family members to appeal a murder conviction. Aaron's now-former client, Oscar Renee Sandoval, was sentenced to life in prison in February 2025 after being convicted of killing Shiereen Al-Jibury, who was his partner and the mother of his children.
